reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / Fitzpatrick's Dermatology
clinicalPearls: A papulosquamous disorder characterised by orange-red scaly plaques, follicular hyperkeratotic papules, and a waxy palmoplantar keratoderma
Classic clues are well-demarcated 'islands of sparing' of normal skin within an otherwise widespread erythema that may progress to erythroderma
Follicular papules with central keratotic plugs, often giving a nutmeg-grater texture on the dorsal fingers, are highly suggestive
A cephalocaudal spread starting on the head and neck is typical of the classic adult form
Griffiths classification divides it into six types by age of onset, extent, and features, including HIV-associated disease
Histology shows alternating orthokeratosis and parakeratosis in vertical and horizontal directions ('checkerboard' pattern) with follicular plugging
Many classic adult cases remit spontaneously over a few years, though treatment with systemic retinoids or other agents is often needed
reference.pathophysiology: Pityriasis rubra pilaris is a chronic papulosquamous disorder of keratinisation whose precise cause is uncertain. Abnormal epidermal differentiation and follicular hyperkeratosis produce the characteristic follicular papules, orange-red plaques, and palmoplantar keratoderma. A subset of familial cases is linked to gain-of-function mutations in CARD14, implicating dysregulated innate immune (NF-kappaB) signalling, and acquired cases may follow infection or other immune triggers, including HIV. The disordered maturation of keratinocytes leaves discrete areas of preserved skin, producing the diagnostic islands of sparing.
additionalDifferentials: Erythroderma of other cause (drug reaction, cutaneous lymphoma)
Follicular ichthyosis or other disorders of keratinisation
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy showing alternating ortho- and parakeratosis with follicular plugging
HIV testing given the recognised association with type VI disease
Assessment for erythroderma complications including fluid balance and temperature regulation
Exclusion of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma in atypical or refractory erythroderma
Baseline liver function and lipids before systemic retinoid therapy
Review for CARD14-associated familial disease where inherited pattern is suggested
redFlags: Erythroderma with impaired thermoregulation, fluid loss, and high-output cardiac failure
Secondary infection or sepsis of extensively involved skin
Rapidly progressive or atypical disease raising concern for cutaneous lymphoma
New-onset severe disease prompting consideration of underlying HIV infection
reference.prognosis: The classic adult form often resolves spontaneously within one to several years, whereas other subtypes, particularly juvenile-onset familial and HIV-associated disease, tend to be more chronic and refractory.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing it as psoriasis and missing the islands of sparing and follicular papules
Overlooking HIV as an underlying driver in severe or atypical presentations
Failing to recognise and manage the systemic risks of erythroderma
Not considering cutaneous T-cell lymphoma in persistent unexplained erythroderma
management: Oral retinoids such as acitretin or isotretinoin as first-line systemic therapy
Methotrexate as a second-line systemic agent, alone or combined with a retinoid
Biologic therapy with TNF inhibitors, ustekinumab or IL-17 inhibitors for refractory disease, particularly CARD14-associated cases
Topical emollients, keratolytics, corticosteroids and vitamin D analogues for skin comfort and scaling
Supportive care of erythroderma with attention to fluid balance, temperature regulation and skin-barrier protection
HIV testing and antiretroviral therapy where type VI disease is identified
Monitoring of liver function and lipids during systemic retinoid therapy
Dermatology-led follow-up, excluding cutaneous T-cell lymphoma in refractory erythroderma
